title: Sex Differences in Cardiometabolic Health and Disease
text:
OVERALL: Sex Differences in the Cardiometabolic Health and Disease
NARRATIVE
Men and women differ in their risk for the development of cardiometabolic diseases, and in their response to
widely used preventive drugs. We are dedicated to understanding the reasons for these sex differences, and
will study the effects of hormones and genetic factors. Our studies will allow the development of therapies that
will optimally benefit both women and men.

title: Southern California Undiagnosed Disease Network
text: The SoCal UDN will serve as a regional Diagnostic Center of Excellence within the national UDN and will offer in-depth expert clinical and research evaluation to improve the diagnosis and care for patients with undiagnosed diseases. We will partner with regional referral centers as well as community programs to expand access to UDN expertise to patients throughout the southwestern US with an emphasis on medically underserved populations. This program will advance our understanding of rare disease pathogenesis and improve the diagnostic process.

title: Optic Nerve Relays for Vision Restoration and Advancement Optic Nerve Regeneration Research
text:
The disruption of connections between the eye and the brain causes irreversible vision loss. The proposed
research will develop the novel use of stem cell therapies and nerve relays to restore the lost connections
between the eye and the brain and enable whole eye transplants. This is relevant to public health because
restoring vision and reversing blindness would significantly improve the lives of individuals blinded by optic
neuropathies or retinal disease.

title: LAMPS
text:
Core 3 will provide new technology platforms by incorporating CRISPR-based chromatin purification,
optogenetics, and multi-omic approaches to dissect the relationships between fusion oncoprotein-mediated
condensate formation, chromatin dysregulation, and oncogenic gene transcription in multiple pediatric cancers.
All Projects will be supported by this Core.

title: Understanding Mammalian Golgi Trafficking Mechanisms
text:
This project will study molecular mechanisms by which intracellular protein sorting is regulated by proteins and
lipids at the Golgi complex, and how this results in targeting of proteins to the cell surface and other locations.
The work will be important for understanding cancer, neuropathies and other human diseases.

title: Human Microbiome Compendium: large-scale curation and processing ofhuman microbiome datasets
text:
This project aims to expand the Human Microbiome Compendium by integrating more than one million samples
of human microbiome data into a unified dataset that characterizes sample content and host information at a
level far more specific and searchable than that of the NCBI databases in which they're stored. Researchers will
be able to retrieve and analyze sequence-level information about the microbial composition of each sample,
paired with information built using state-of-the-art machine learning techniques. The objectives of this proposal
are consistent with the NOFO for curation at scale for biomedical research assets—in addition to generating the
largest dataset of its kind for human microbiome data, this project will also develop automation approaches and
software tools that will enable others to build compendia of their own using publicly available data.

title: Neurodevelopmental effects of flame retardant exposure
text:
Anthropogenic chemicals are likely contributing to rising rates of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) with
socioemotional deficits, but the vast majority of work on NDDs to date has focused on genetic rather than
environmental risk factors. Here we employ an animal model of social behavior, the prairie vole, to investigate
how developmental exposure to a widespread environmental chemical contaminate impacts areas of the nervous
system relevant to two behavioral traits common to many NDDs: anxiety and sociality. To achieve this goal, we
focus on a widely-used flame retardant mixture implicated in human and animal studies known to contribute to
a wide variety of sex-specific adverse effects on socioemotional related behaviors.

title: Dynamic Treatment Regimes for Personalized Opioid Use Disorder Care
text:
The proposed research aims to improve opioid use disorder (OUD) treatment quality by using machine
learning dynamic treatment regime models (DTRs) that measure the time-varying relationship between
treatment and patient-reported OUD severity to identify optimal practice patterns. Several DTR models will be
estimated and compared in terms of their ability to identify treatment decision rules that minimize patient risk of
fatal and non-fatal opioid overdose, and a pilot hybrid factorial sequential multiple assignment trial (SMART)
will be conducted to assess the feasibility and acceptability of a full-scale trial that will evaluate the
effectiveness of the generated treatment decision rules. The research aligns with NIDA's strategic goals by
promising significant advancements in OUD treatment quality and the broader field of personalized medicine
for chronic substance use disorders.

title: Cancer Research Training and Education Coordination (CRTEC)
text: The Duke Cancer Institute’s Cancer Research Training and Education Coordination (CRTEC) works in close partnership with the Duke University School of Medicine and Duke University Health System. Together these entities provide a rich, collaborative academic environment committed to education, training, research, and clinical care of cancer patients. DCI CRTEC is led by Gerard Blobe, MD, PhD (PCMIT), Professor of Medicine, Pharmacology and Cancer Biology. He is a physician-scientist with laboratory and clinical research experience and director of the Lefkowitz Society - a post-graduate mentoring program for physician-scientists. The activities of DCI CRTEC and Blobe are supported by CRTEC Assistant Director, Kathryn Dickerson, PhD and CRTEC Program Manager, Colleen Bauer, MA as well as an Oversight Committee consisting of DCI members, Duke faculty and trainee representatives. Blobe reports to the DCI Executive Director and to the DCI Executive Committee and chairs the DCI CRTEC Oversight Committee. DCI CRTEC’s mission is to decrease the burden of cancer by facilitating the training of a broad cohort of cancer researchers and care providers across the training continuum, from high school students to junior faculty. The DCI CRTEC supports over 1,450 trainees engaged in cancer-related research and clinical care with a comprehensive range of educational, mentoring, and career development resources. From 2019-2023 the DCI has made direct investments of $4.1 million dollars in training and education. CRTEC works closely with Tomi Akinyemiju, PhD (CRDI), Associate Director of the DCI Community Outreach and Engagement (COE), including collaboratively initiating and implementing two new post-baccalaureate programs: the DIRECT Cancer Fellowship Program and NIGMS R25 funded PRIME-PREP. New CRTEC initiatives since prior review include an NCI R25 funded PRIME Summer Research Program, an NCI R25 funded Bioinformatics Course, and NCI R38 funded Radiation Oncology Research In Residency Program, an Internal Grant Review mechanism for DCI trainees and members, a new library of NIH funded grants (F, K and supplements), a Cancer Biology Journal Club, a CRTEC Training and Education Newsletter, trainee listservs, a DCI Onboarding Resource, and regular Drop-In Socials for the DCI community, including trainees and members.

title: Influenza Modeling of Correlates of Protection for Optimal Immune Dynamics and Evolution.
text:
We will use early and longitudinal multi-OMIC datasets and longitudinal innate, cellular and humoral immune
responses to identify novel correlates of protection beyond neutralizing antibodies. Computational modeling and
will validate the best signatures of immune protection.

title: Nutrient signaling at ER-Mitochondrial contacts and age-related mitochondrial dysfunction
text:
Altered mitochondrial networking and energetics contributes to age-related diseases. Maintenance of
mitochondrial networking is a function of the balance between rates of mitochondrial fission and fusion, which
is, in turn, regulated by proteins localized at endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondria contacts or MAMs. Studies
in this application will advance our understanding of the interplay between mTORC2 kinase and its
downstream targets at MAMs in preventing age-related decline in mitochondrial fission and energetics.

title: Data Science Shared Resource
text: The application of next generation sequencing and machine learning methods has revolutionized the field of cancer research, providing more opportunities for investigating tumor heterogeneity and its interaction with the tumor microenvironment. However, this vast amount of data also presents major challenges in handling, analyzing, and interpreting them. Thus, the Data Science Shared Resource (DSSR) of the Simmons Comprehensive Cancer Center (SCCC) was established in 2010 with the goal of providing comprehensive informatics, data analytics, data integration, and data management support for SCCC members. Specifically, the DSSR provides (1) access to high-performance computing systems, (2) support for bioinformatics analyses, including pre-processing, analysis, and biological interpretation of high-throughput molecular data, (3) support for data integration including integrative analysis and biomarker discovery, (4) support for data management and data submission, as well as facilitating members’ use of public dataset and data mining process, (5) data science support for grant applications, and (6) computational pipelines distribution and education/training. DSSR has successfully implemented several cancer data commons for breast, kidney, liver, and lung, which are key research areas in SCCC, in addition to the development of customized computational pipelines for all SCCC members. The DSSR team consists of one bioinformatics faculty and five computational biologists, who are experts in analyzing various types of NGS data, such as genomics (WGS/WES), epigenomics (ATAC-seq, single-cell ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN, and ChIP-seq), transcriptomics (bulk and single-cell RNA-seq), and multi- omics (CITE-seq) data as well as proteomics/metabolomics data. The team also can assist with developing machine learning/deep learning (ML/DL) models and biomedical image analysis. During the current grant cycle, the DSSR provided services to 91 SCCC members and contributed to 230 cancer-relevant publications, including the work published in high-impact journals such as Nature, Cancer Cell, Cell, Science, Cancer Discovery, Nature Methods, and Blood. DSSR services are successfully delivered by the accumulated experience of the staff, as well as customized and innovative approaches in solving problems encountered in data analysis. With strong support from SCCC, the DSSR provides extensive services to SCCC members, providing key contributions to meeting the research needs and mission of SCCC.

title: Integrated fatty acid profiling unveils a linkage between BMI and efficacy of anti-tumor immunotherapy
text:
A comprehensive understanding of why mildly obese individuals achieve better outcomes when receiving
immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) treatment remains elusive. Employing innovative screening methodologies,
our study reveals the distinctive role of circulating essential fatty acids (EFAs) as potent immunomodulators,
reprogramming CD8+ T cell functionality, and anti-tumor immunity. This K99/R00 initiative seeks to elucidate the
underlying mechanisms behind the enhanced response of mildly obese cancer patients to immunotherapy, and
to provide novel insights into the development of immunomodulators to improve the clinical outcomes of
immunotherapy.

title: Expedited Assessment of Environment-induced Respiratory Ciliopathies Leveraging Motile Apical-out Airway Organoids
text:
This proposal will develop computer vision tools to augment a motile, cilia-powered, lung organoid platform,
combining tissue engineering with computational analysis to present a complete bioengineering platform that
accurately captures organoid motility and underlying cilia (dys)function. The goal of the current proposal is to
utilize this platform to recapitulate the effects of pollution particulates on the lung epithelium, paving the way for
personalized assessment of respiratory injury.

title: Building Safety Guards into LLMs for Trustworthy Automatic Simplification of Medical Documents
text:
This proposal concerns the development of natural language processing methods and tools that
establish essential guardrails to the safe use of large language models (LLMs) when used to
simplify medical texts. The premise is that LLMs oﬀer the tantalizing opportunity to enable lay
access to newly published evidence, but current models risk introducing inaccurate information
into automatically simpliﬁed texts; this proposal concerns designing techniques that mitigate
such risk. These kinds of “safe generation” techniques have the potential to empower users with
the ability to critically read LLM outputs; our immediate, important aim is to enable access to
trustworthy plain language summaries of medical evidence, but the developed methods will
have application in similar contexts where “safe” generation is critical.

title: Calmodulin and Regulation of Cardiac Ryanodine Receptor and CaMKII
text:
Heart failure and arrhythmias are major human health issues, afflicting millions of Americans. It has become
clear that leak of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum within the cardiac myocyte between normal heart
beats contributes importantly to both of these major cardiac problems, as does the chronic activation of the
calcium-dependent enzyme CaMKII. Here we will elucidate the structural and functional properties and
problem that occur at the molecular and myocyte level, and develop novel therapeutic strategies.

title: Comparative vertebrate neural crest contribution to the hematopoietic stem cell specification niche
text:
The only therapy for many hematological disorders such as leukemia depends on hematopoietic stem cells
(HSCs) – cells that give rise to the entire blood system of an organism – which are limited by the availability of
compatible donors. This proposal aims to understand how a transient embryonic population of migratory neural
crest cells directs HSC formation in vertebrates. Understanding this process will provide critical insights for
optimizing HSCs generation in vitro for biomedical applications.

title: Identifying actionable multilevel intervention strategies to improve cardiovascular health among people with HIV
text:
People with HIV experience higher rates of cardiovascular disease that are not fully explained by
HIV-related clinical factors alone. This project will identify combinations of social, behavioral,
healthcare access, and community factors associated with cardiovascular disease and use those
findings to develop and evaluate actionable intervention targets. The results will inform solution oriented
implementation strategies to improve cardiovascular health among people with HIV that
can be applied to other affected populations.

title: Developing a Suite of Targeted Anticancer Drugs
text:
‘Personalized’ drugs for cancer exploit specific alterations in the cancer cell, for example a mutated,
overexpressed, or fused protein that is present in tumor cells but not normal cells, but only a handful of
such drugs are available and the pace of development is slow. We have implemented a strategy that
enables discovery of novel compounds that are selective for certain cancer subtypes, leading to 4 of our
anticancer drugs moving toward clinical trials in the last 15 years. As described herein, we will now
accelerate this discovery platform, utilizing a novel compound collection biased for selective anticancer
activity; this strategy will allow us and others to discover and develop scores of new cancer drugs that
are matched to specific molecular defects in a patient’s tumor.

title: Using Bioinformatics Methodologies to Explore the Role of Short Interspersed Elements in the Pathogenesis of Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies
text:
Short interspersed elements are a type of genomic repeats that can form double stranded RNA capable of
activating the immune system in a way similar to that of a viral state. We will study the role of these repeats in
idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, which can lead to new insights into the molecular nature of disease and
ultimately lead to better therapeutics. In the long term, this can also lead to a better understanding of
autoimmunity.
